title: So every good work belongs to piety and in its way profits salvation
source_text: XLIV. Porro cum, ex Jansenii mente, nullum sit bonum opus quod non ex coelesti quadam charitate profluat, atque ad Deum in aeterna vita possidendum non referatur, inde quoque consequens est, nullum esse bonum opus, quod non ad Dei cultum & pietatem pertineat, & suo modo prosit ad animae salutem. Adeoque frustra Scholasticos distinguere bona opera in ea quae solum moraliter bona sunt, nec possunt inter actus pietatis & religionis censeri; ac proinde facienti nihil prosunt ad vitam aeternam: & ea in quibus pietas & religio consistit, & quae sic ad salutem animae & vitam aeternam aliquid conferunt.
pass_a_gloss: XLIV. Further since, from the mind of Jansenius, there is no good work which flows not from a certain heavenly charity, and is not referred to God to be possessed in eternal life, thence also it is consequent, that there is no good work, which pertains not to the worship of God and piety, and in its manner profits to the salvation of the soul. And so in vain do the Schoolmen distinguish good works into those which are only morally good, and cannot be reckoned among acts of piety and religion; and therefore profit the doer nothing to eternal life: and those in which piety and religion consist, and which so confer something to the salvation of the soul and eternal life.
pass_b_english: Further, since in Jansenius's mind there is no good work that does not flow from a kind of heavenly charity and is not referred to God, to be possessed in eternal life, it also follows that there is no good work that does not belong to the worship of God and to piety and in its own way profit the soul's salvation.

So the Schoolmen divide good works in vain into those that are only morally good, cannot be counted among acts of piety and religion, and so profit the doer nothing toward eternal life, and those in which piety and religion consist and which in this way contribute something to the soul's salvation and eternal life.

choices.why: The theological virtue by which God is loved for his own sake; Jansenius sets it against cupiditas as the only two loves, so the technical 'charity' is kept rather than 'love'.
